claims.text: Short sleep duration is significantly associated with an increased risk of depression in adults.
Long sleep duration is significantly associated with an increased risk of depression in adults.
The associations between sleep duration and risk of depression do not substantially change in sensitivity and subgroup analyses.
No evidence of publication bias was found among the included prospective studies.

evidence.description: The pooled RR for depression was 1.31 (95% CI, 1.04-1.64; I(2) = 0%) for short sleep duration across 25,271 participants.
The pooled RR for depression was 1.42 (95% CI, 1.04-1.92; I(2) = 0%) for long sleep duration across 23,663 participants.
Sensitivity and subgroup analyses showed that the associations between short or long sleep duration and risk of depression did not substantially change.
Statistical testing indicated no evidence of publication bias across the seven included studies.

methodologies.name: Random-effects meta-analysis
methodologies.description: Systematic literature search of PubMed and Web of Science followed by random-effects meta-analysis to calculate pooled relative risks.

limitations.text: Results from longitudinal studies on sleep duration and incidence of depression remain controversial.
